newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Used clothes take over Central American style.
newsitem.headline: Used clothes take over Central American style.

text.p: Until recently, even poor Central Americans felt too ashamed to wear someone else's discarded clothes.

But now, unable to resist $1 to $2 price tags on dresses, Guatemalans, Salvadorans, Hondurans and Costa Ricans of all backgrounds paw through gigantic piles of clothes at thousands of used-clothes stores that have proliferated since the mid- 1980s.

In Costa Rica the middle class is getting in on the used clothes act. Sergio Chacon, an office manager for a bank, said he could not afford the suits that are obligatory at his office and that cost a minimum of $150 each.
His mother suggested he shop at the "Ropa Americana" stores, as used-clothing businesses are known there, and now he is the best-dressed man in the office, sporting $3 suits.

More than 90 percent of the used clothes come in bales from the United States, from brokers who buy overstock, customer returns, clothes unsold in department stores, and donations to charities such as Salvation Army and Goodwill.
In El Salvador, the origin of the clothes inspired the name of a chain of used-clothes stores -- USA-2.
"Ninety percent of Guatemalans are consuming these clothes, because new clothes are so expensive. Only the high class doesn't buy it," said importer Patricia Milian.
Guatemala's imports of used clothes have increased sevenfold since 1988, from about 2.2 million pounds (1 million kg) to 15.4 million pounds (7 million kg).

In El Salvador, used clothes imports tripled between 1993 and 1996. "The demand for used clothing in Latin America and worldwide is tenfold what it was three years ago. I think it has a lot to do with lowering of tariffs and restrictions," Carl Jones, a used clothes exporter in California, said.
Not everyone is happy about the "pacas," (Spanish for bales) as used-clothes stores are known in Guatemala.

"Imports of used clothes are a competition that harms our small garment industry. We have asked for higher duties on these imports," said Rafael Cruz, president of the Honduran Association of Small and Medium Clothesmaking Industries.
Business groups in Costa Rica, El Salvador and Guatemala echo the calls for higher import duties on used clothes.

"They are taking advantage of poverty. Maybe for the United States this is some type of recycling and they think they are doing people a favour, but they're just ruining the economy," said Donald Rodas, who makes t-shirts and underwear in his struggling home factory in Guatemala City.
According to Rodas, cheap used clothes have pushed him and other manufacturers to the verge of bankruptcy. Since 1991 he has gone from employing 60 to 16 people, he said.
In addition, the Guatemalan Chamber of Industry blames used clothes imports for the closing of 55 cloth mills in Guatemala since 1990, doing away with 50,000 direct and indirect jobs.

Rodas leads an association of small manufacturers pushing for higher tariffs. The group has persuaded the government to form an economic commission to study the matter, but government officials say they will not block imports.
"It is very difficult to justify prohibiting used clothes imports so the line of thought is to regulate, not prohibit," said Economy Minister Juan Mauricio Wurmser.
He said regulation will not mean higher tarrifs, but stiffer health standards as well as better control at customs and opening bales to ensure no new clothes are hidden inside.
Reni Bake, executive director of the textile guild of the Chamber of Industry, said her organisation supports that sort of regulation.
But Milian, manager of Trans Global Recycling, one of 12 big importers that bring in 70 percent of Guatemala's used clothes, is fighting any sort of restrictions.
She said she cannot afford to rebale clothes if they are opened, and she said the 30 percent import tax on an estimated minimum price of 36 cents a pound of used clothes, is high enough.

Milian said it costs $300 to import a bale of "guaranteed acceptable quality" clothes which she sells for an average $600 to rural entrepreneurs who drive bales out to small towns to sell out of the back of their pickups on market day.

Milian and other importers in Central America buy from brokers such as Jones' Southern Textile company in California, which sells 100 pound (45 kg) bales for an average of 85 cents a pound ($1.85 per kg).
Jones, said he believed Latin American countries are best off adopting an open market strategy.
"If they would lighten up and let these guys do business, the market will tell them what to do," said Jones.
